interactions.title: Seeker recounts Frankar’s disappearance
lines: Seeker: I can start. So, Seeker’s crouched, brooding, grinding two stones together in his fists. Nice. Begins to speak. I, I have—or had—a younger brother. Do not know for certain.

Seeker: Frankar was his name. We called him Frank. I was thinking of him and in the storm and all those days that he spent hunting the strange white salamanders. Frank was a wonderful kid, a prodigy, wise beyond his years. My younger brother, he, he memorized the architectural histories. He could draw a diagram of the entire great keep from memory. He was the pride of our parents. Yeah, he was a talent in the runic magic too, he—something that comes along just once in a generation. He was fluent with the symbols, like he was conducting music, but the musicians were the arches of stone around us.

Seeker: Frank had a dark side too. He was obsessed with perfection. And he became obsessed with a game—strange game that he had invented. It was a kind of divination, but without the gods. I think a way, or so he thought, to know what lay in the future so that he could never fail. It was a kind of machine made of stone wheels and bits of crystal and gemstone, animated by magic, but it was an evil machine. It was like the face of a great clock. Clock. He would place at the center a tiny white salamander, a blind creature, of a rare thing you only find deep underground. He was always hunting these tiny white salamanders.

Seeker: The salamander would enter the clock from its center and crawl about, sealed inside, seeking a way out. And around the face of the clock of stone were 12 tiny passages, and if the salamander went this one way out, it would be frozen to death. And another way, it would be crushed between two cleverly arranged stones, and a different way and it would be sliced in two by a blade and, or suffocated, or shocked, and so on. Depending on the fate of the salamander, Frank would know the future. If the salamander is crushed, then perhaps some great crushing weight would come upon him. Or if he was stabbed, perhaps there would be a heartbreak, or perhaps some great insight. Who knows if it really worked to tell the future?

Seeker: Frank's machine was was a secret from us. You see, he carefully hid it from everyone. We only learned about it one morning, the morning after the night of a great raging storm. We found the machine at the very top of the keep, high above the mountain, all, all in pieces. By careful study and reconstruction of it, I determined what it had been and what it had been for—or or so I think. Frank, my beloved little brother, he was, he was gone that day. We don't know where he went, and we have not seen him since. The only clue he left behind: the tiny white salamander, burnt to a crisp.
Kenzo: How long ago was that, Seeker?
Seeker: Frank—Frank was only an adolescent at that time, and I just a few years older.
Kenzo: How many years has it been since you've seen him?
Seeker: Could be like 20 or 30 years ago.
DM: So like 30 years ago. Yeah.
Kenzo: And just vanished. So he's out there someplace.
Seeker: Maybe it killed him. Maybe he went out in the storm. We don't know. I'd like to think that he's someplace good. I wish I knew.

before: Delwath: Yeah.

Just to the north, trapped in a tower and his own mind, the storm giant Hralgar brings an unnatural storm to the plains, lightning and thunder ever present, the danger of fire reduced here only by the fact that there is little left to burn on this part of the plains.

DM: Somewhere to the west—not far to the west at this point—a dwarf and a human ride together in tense silence, heading for Tokra, where the dwarf will turn south for her people in the rocky mountains and the human will turn northwest for her home in Chardon, returning with news of Agata Dustmother. To the south, Dunmari ride: Alesh and her companions returning to Karawa with news of the south, unsure of what they will find in the small hometown of the Mystai of Shakun; Havdar’s small band of warriors riding across the plains to protect the people and hunt gnolls.

DM: Somewhere, you hope, the thousands of families leaving their homes and heading west, joining the slow march of the citizens of Karawa, hoping to outrun and outlast the new danger of these plains behind the banks of the River Hara. From the east, the dry winds blowing from the blasted plains and desolation of Cha’mutte bring no news.

DM: As the exhaustion and tiredness of the escape from the storm sink over you, and as you enjoy a peaceful breakfast resting in the clear morning air, memories of your childhood begin to overtake you. And you find yourself beginning to tell a story to these companions whose lives you have saved many times over the past month now, but whom you still don't really know that much about. So, who wants to start?

You don't... It's been a long time since I've been in my homeland and had any of my native food, but as a child... Baking for my...
Unknown: What?

Delwath: Elves don't really have big families, I assume. No, yeah, like there would be very few elven kids at any given time, I assume. Yeah. Yeah, I’m—baking for the for the elders of of our of our home was my one of my favorite activities. They would... Children were rare. I was the only, only young one of my age in the town, you know, in our community and…

Delwath: You elves—at that time, it was a it was a dark time, the—the rumors of hobgoblins and orcs were moving across the land, and this great darkness that she brought was starting to spread and few were interested in the old traditions and the old foods and keeping to our ways. Everybody talked of the outside world and the the change that's coming, and the end of an age is near. And all I wanted to do is cook for those folks who... I listen to the stories they told and appreciated their wisdom.

Delwath: I remember learning how to cook the sisila tree, which, not being elves yourselves, none of you have tasted it, but the fruit itself takes years to mature. And so usually you only get a few opportunities every couple decades to to cook one of these, these cakes. And the honor and importance I felt as a youngster being allowed to take the fruit and bake one of the cakes for our celebration was a feeling I miss, a feeling of home that really I have not felt in many, many years. Delwath kind of crumbles the food. This is not the same as the food at home.

lines: Kenzo: I feel similarly about Chardon. It was not a good place for a kid like me in a place like that. A lot of magic, but not for everyone, only for folks like the Society of the Open Scroll and I think... I have a feeling we're going to end up there at some point before for long, but...

Kenzo: If you were of the right lineage and from the right family, Chardon can be a very, very special place. But I think for young people like myself, my friends, you know, the idea of magic, I think, was much more, you know, dealing with the toxic waste from the chalyte refineries. Seeing what magic for the elites meant for us and the strange aftereffects from all the experiments that we would see in our neighborhood. So I feel like got a lot of mixed feelings about about Chardon and potentially journeying there. But something about it calls to me still, I think.

Kenzo: When I think about my friends from growing up, it was about survival. It wasn't about trying to learn scholarship or trying to understand mysteries of nature or consciousness or anything else. I mean, I feel very lucky now that I've been able to escape, in some ways. But there's a terrible imbalance in a place like Chardon, the terrible imbalance that I think for so many that live there is, is a poison, is a deep, deep poison, a physical poison and also a spiritual one. And I'm wary of these items, you know. Kenzo kind of glances around it like the mirror and in these other these other tools.

Kenzo: I feel like we, we take magic and these games of the soul, and these other planes of existence, in ways that we don't fully understand and for results that are horrible for so many people like myself when I was a little boy. So I worry. I worry about the fact that these items are reappearing, and I worry about where they're going to end up and the impact they're going to have on, on the children like me, who grew up in places where there weren’t families and there weren’t warm hearths to sit around and feel like you had a home. interactions.title: Wellby remembers his family and great-great-grandfather
lines: Wellby: Toward the firelight. As a child, among the family, among my people, it always seemed that the concerns of men and elves and dwarves were alien things. To speak of home and imagine going back to it again. Um, my parents told me that until the time I was 10, we never stepped on the same piece of soil twice. We went from one side of the Green Sea to the other in flat-bottom river boats. We went up every river in Sembara, all the way to the mountains, back down again, and spent seasons in Tollen, Cymea. Saw the swamps.

Wellby: My great-great-grandfather was a storyteller, and when we'd go from place to place, he would tell us that all places are one place. And he would tell us stories of things that happened long, long ago and say that all times are one time.

Wellby: The season that he died was the same season that my family stopped walking on new soil. They found a comfortable route, caravan roads between safe cities. It's a good thing for them. But I remember standing on the deck with him that summer, and he would look down into the darkness at the bottom of the waves. And soon, in the days before he died, he said that he could remember them, that he could remember the specific waves, that he'd seen them before. And he greeted them by name like old friends.

Wellby: I spent years going around and around on the roads and learning to shoot and fight and hide and track and scout for my family, my people. But I knew that I couldn't stay there, and I needed to feel new dirt under my feet again. I never understood what he meant when he would say that, that all places are one place. But hearing you, now I understand it better. I'm already home. For my people, the road is the home. There's no going back. There's only going forward. That's what he would say.
